'''NOMINATE''' (an acronym for ''nominal three-step estimation'') is a [[multidimensional scaling]] application developed by US [[Political science|political scientists]] [[Keith T. Poole]] and [[Howard Rosenthal (political scientist)|Howard Rosenthal]] in the early 1980s to analyze preferential and choice data, such as [[Voting methods in deliberative assemblies#Recorded vote|legislative roll-call voting]] behavior.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Poole|first1=Keith T.|first2=Howard|last2=Rosenthal|year=1983|url=http://k7moa.com/pdf/Upside_Down-A_Spatial_Model_for_Legislative_Roll_Call_Analysis_1983.pdf|title=A Spatial Model for Legislative Roll Call Analysis|journal=GSIA Working Paper No. 5–83–84}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Poole|first1=Keith T.|first2=Howard|last2=Rosenthal|title=A Spatial Model For Legislative Roll Call Analysis|journal=American Journal of Political Science|year=1985|volume=29|issue=2|pages=357–384|doi=10.2307/2111172|jstor=2111172|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/81716/1/sswp487.pdf}}</ref> In its most well-known application, members of the US Congress are placed on a two-dimensional map, with politicians who are ideologically similar (i.e. who often vote the same) being close together. One of these two dimensions corresponds to the familiar [[left–right political spectrum]] (liberal–conservative in the United States).

As computing capabilities grew, Poole and Rosenthal developed multiple iterations of their NOMINATE procedure: the original D-NOMINATE method, W-NOMINATE, and most recently DW-NOMINATE (for dynamic, weighted NOMINATE). In 2009, Poole and Rosenthal were the first recipients of the [[Society for Political Methodology]]'s Best Statistical Software Award for their development of NOMINATE.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Awards |url=http://polmeth.wustl.edu/about.php?page=awards |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100620171509/http://polmeth.wustl.edu/about.php?page=awards |archive-date=20 June 2010 |website=The Society for Political Methodology}}</ref> In 2016, the society awarded Poole its Career Achievement Award, stating that "the modern study of the U.S. Congress would be simply unthinkable without NOMINATE legislative roll call voting scores."<ref name=":1">{{cite web |title=The 2016 Political Methodology Career Achievement Award: Keith T. Poole |url=https://polmeth.wustl.edu/career-achievement-award/articles/1443 |website=The Society for Political Methodology}}</ref>

==Procedure==
The main procedure is an application of [[multidimensional scaling]] techniques to political choice data. Though there are important technical differences between these types of NOMINATE scaling procedures,<ref>[http://k7moa.com/page2a.htm Description of NOMINATE Data].</ref> all operate under the same fundamental assumptions. First, that alternative choices can be projected on a basic, low-dimensional (often two-dimensional) [[Euclidean space]]. Second, within that space, individuals have utility functions which are bell-shaped ([[Normal distribution|normally distributed]]), and maximized at their ideal point. Because individuals also have symmetric, single-peaked [[Utility|utility functions]] which center on their ideal point, ideal points represent individuals' most preferred outcomes. That is, individuals most desire outcomes closest their ideal point, and will choose/vote probabilistically for the closest outcome.

Ideal points can be recovered from observing choices, with individuals exhibiting similar preferences placed more closely than those behaving dissimilarly. It is helpful to compare this procedure to producing maps based on driving distances between cities. For example, Los Angeles is about 1,800 miles from St. Louis; St. Louis is about 1,200 miles from Miami; and Miami is about 2,700 miles from Los Angeles. From this (dis)similarities data, any map of these three cities should place Miami far from Los Angeles, with St. Louis somewhere in between (though a bit closer to Miami than Los Angeles).  Just as cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco would be clustered on a map, NOMINATE places ideologically similar [[Legislator|legislators]] (e.g., liberal Senators [[Barbara Boxer|Barbara Boxer (D-Calif.)]] and [[Al Franken|Al Franken (D-Minn.)]]) closer to each other, and farther from dissimilar legislators (e.g., conservative Senator [[Tom Coburn|Tom Coburn (R-Okla.)]]) based on the degree of agreement between their roll call voting records. At the heart of the NOMINATE procedures (and other [[Multidimensional scaling|multidimensional scaling methods]], such as Poole's Optimal Classification method<ref name="Poole2005">{{cite book|last=Poole|first=Keith T.|title=Spatial Models of Parliamentary Voting|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OmeQNHvcULoC|access-date=9 November 2012|year=2005|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-85194-7|pages=46–}}</ref>) are algorithms they utilize to arrange individuals and choices in low dimensional (usually two-dimensional) space. Thus, NOMINATE scores provide "maps" of legislatures.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.slate.com/id/2060047/|title=Mapping Congress' growing polarization|last=Ellenberg|first=Jordan|date=26 December 2001|work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|access-date=9 November 2012}}</ref>

[[File:Me and howard 1984 4.gif|thumb|left|Keith T. Poole (left) and Howard Rosenthal (right), 1984.]]
Using NOMINATE procedures to study congressional roll call voting behavior from the [[1st United States Congress|First Congress]] to the
present-day, Poole and Rosenthal published ''Congress: A Political-Economic History of Roll Call Voting''<ref>{{cite book|last1=Poole|first1=Keith T.|first2=Howard|last2=Rosenthal|year=1997|title=Congress: A Political-Economic History of Roll Call Voting|location=New York|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> in 1997 and the revised edition ''Ideology and Congress''<ref>{{cite book|last1=Poole|first1=Keith T.|first2=Howard|last2=Rosenthal|year=2007|title=Ideology and Congress|location=New Brunswick, NJ|publisher=Transaction Publishers|url=http://www.transactionpub.com/title/Ideology-and%20Congress-978-1-4128-0608-4.html}}</ref> in 2007. 

In 2009, Poole and Rosenthal were named the first recipients of the [[Society for Political Methodology]]'s Best Statistical Software Award for their development of NOMINATE, a recognition conferred to "individual(s) for developing statistical software that makes a significant research contribution".<ref name=":0" /> In 2016, Keith T. Poole was awarded the Society for Political Methodology's Career Achievement Award. The citation for this award reads, in part, "One can say perfectly correctly, and without any hyperbole: the modern study of the U.S. Congress would be simply unthinkable without NOMINATE legislative roll call voting scores. NOMINATE has produced data that entire bodies of our discipline—and many in the press—have relied on to understand the U.S. Congress."<ref name=":1" />

==Dimensions==
Poole and Rosenthal demonstrate that—despite the many complexities of congressional representation and politics—[[Voting methods in deliberative assemblies#Recorded vote|roll call voting]] in both the [[United States House of Representatives|House]] and the [[United States Senate|Senate]] can be organized and explained by no more than two dimensions throughout the sweep of American history. The first dimension (horizontal or x-axis) is the familiar [[Political spectrum|left-right]] (or liberal-conservative) spectrum on economic matters. The second dimension (vertical or y-axis) picks up attitudes on cross-cutting, salient issues of the day (which include or have included [[slavery]], [[bimetallism]], [[Civil and political rights|civil rights]], regional, and social/lifestyle issues). Rosenthal and Poole have initially argued that the first dimension refers to socio-economic matters and the second dimension to race-relations.<ref name="Everson_2000">{{cite journal |last1=Everson |first1=Phil |display-authors=etal |title=NOMINATE and American Political History: A Primer |journal=Vote View Working Paper |date=2009}}</ref> However, the often confusing and residual nature of the second dimension has led to the second dimension being largely ignored by other researchers.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bateman |first1=D |title=Studies in American Political Development 2016 |journal=Studies in American Political Development |date=2016 |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=147–171 |doi=10.1017/S0898588X16000080 |s2cid=31552378 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/studies-in-american-political-development/article/abs/ideal-points-and-american-political-development-beyond-dwnominate/3741B09129E42267E482FEC8796C381A |access-date=1 February 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

For the most part, congressional voting is uni-dimensional, with most of the variation in voting patterns explained by placement along the liberal-conservative first dimension. While the first dimension of the DW-NOMINATE score is able to predict results at 83% accuracy, the addition of the second dimension only increases accuracy to 85%.<ref name="Everson_2000" /> Furthermore, the second dimension only provided a significant increase in accuracy for Congresses 1-99. As late as the 1990s, the second dimension was able to measure [[Partisan (politics)|partisan splits]] in [[abortion]] and [[Right to keep and bear arms|gun rights]] issues. However, a 2017 analysis found that since 1987, the votes of the US Congress had best fit a one-dimensional model, suggesting increasing [[Political polarization in the United States|party polarization]] after 1987.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Keith |first1=Poole |title=The Collapse of the Voting Structure - Possible Big Trouble Ahead |url=https://voteviewblog.com/2017/01/12/the-collapse-of-the-voting-structure-possible-big-trouble-ahead/ |website=Voteview Blog|date=12 January 2017 }}</ref>

==Interpretation of nominate scores==
For illustrative purposes, consider the following plots which use W-NOMINATE scores to scale members of [[Congress of the United States|Congress]] and uses the probabilistic voting model (in which legislators farther from the "cutting line" between "yea" and "nay" outcomes become more likely to vote in the predicted manner) to illustrate some major Congressional votes in the 1990s. Some of these votes, like the House's vote on [[Bill Clinton|President Clinton's]] welfare reform package ([[Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act|the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act of 1996]]) are best modeled through the use of the first (economic [[Left-right politics|liberal-conservative]]) dimension. On the welfare reform vote, nearly all Republicans joined the [[Moderate (politics)|moderate]]-[[Conservatism in the United States|conservative]] bloc of House Democrats in voting for the bill, while opposition was virtually confined to the most [[Liberalism in the United States|liberal]] Democrats in the House. The errors (those representatives on the "wrong" side of the cutting line which separates predicted "yeas" and predicted "nays") are generally close to the cutting line, which is what we would expect. A legislator directly on the cutting line is indifferent between voting "yea" and "nay" on the measure. All members are shown on the left panel of the plot, while only errors are shown on the right panel:

[[File:NOMINATE 2.jpg|House Vote on Welfare Reform (1996)]]

[[Economic ideology]] also dominates the [[Senate of the United States|Senate]] vote on the [[Balanced Budget Amendment|Balanced Budget Amendment of 1995]]:

[[File:NOMINATE 3.jpg|Senate Vote on Balanced Budget Amendment (1995)]]

On other votes, however, a second dimension (which has recently{{When|date=June 2022}} come to represent attitudes on [[Culture war|cultural and lifestyle issues]]) is important. For example, roll call votes on [[gun control]] routinely split party coalitions, with [[Blue Dog Democrats|socially conservative "blue dog" Democrats]] joining most Republicans in opposing additional regulation and [[Rockefeller Republican|socially liberal Republicans]] joining most Democrats in supporting gun control. The addition of the second dimension accounts for these inter-party differences, and the cutting line is more horizontal than vertical (meaning the cleavage is found on the second dimension rather than the first dimension on these votes) This pattern was evident in the 1991 House vote to require waiting periods on handguns:

[[File:NOMINATE 4.jpg|House Vote on Handgun Waiting Period (1991)]]

==Political ideology==
DW-NOMINATE scores have been used widely to describe the political ideology of political actors, political parties and political institutions.<ref>{{cite book|last=McCarty|first=Nolan|year=2011|chapter=Measuring Legislative Preferences|title=Oxford Handbook of Congress|editor1-first=Eric|editor1-last=Schickler|editor2-first=Frances|editor2-last=Lee|location=Oxford|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> For instance, a score in the first dimension that is close to either pole means that such score is located at one of the extremes in the liberal-conservative scale. So, a score closer to 1 is described as conservative whereas a score closer to −1 can be described as liberal. Finally, a score at zero or close to zero is described as moderate.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Fleisher|first1=Richard |first2=John R.|last2=Bond|year=2004|title=The Shrinking Middle in the US Congress|journal=British Journal of Political Science|volume=34|issue=3|pages=429–451|jstor=4092328|doi=10.1017/s0007123404000122|s2cid=153856544 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Poole|first1=Keith T.|first2=Howard|last2=Rosenthal|year=1997|title=Congress: A Political-Economic History of Roll Call Voting|location=Oxford|publisher=Oxford University Press|at=Appendix}}</ref>

==Political polarization==
[[File:NOMINATE polarization.jpg|thumb|right|Political polarization in the United States House of Representatives.]]
Poole and Rosenthal (beginning with their 1984 article "The Polarization of American Politics"<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Poole|first1=Keith T. |first2=Howard|last2=Rosenthal|year=1984|title=The Polarization of American Politics|journal=Journal of Politics|volume=46|issue=4|pages=1061–79|url=http://k7moa.com/pdf/ThePolarizationofAmericanPolitics_1984.pdf|jstor=2131242|doi=10.2307/2131242|s2cid=19531769 }}</ref>) have also used NOMINATE data to show that, since the 1970s, party delegations in Congress have become ideologically homogeneous and distant from one another (a phenomenon known as "[[Political polarization|polarization]]"). Using DW-NOMINATE scores (which permit direct comparisons between members of different Congresses across time), political scientists have demonstrated the expansion of ideological divides in Congress, which has spurred intense partisanship between Republicans and Democrats in recent{{When|date=June 2022}} decades.<ref>{{cite book|last=Theriault|first=Sean M.|year=2008|title=Party Polarization in Congress|location=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Jacobson|first=Gary|year=2010|title=A Divider, Not a Uniter: George W. Bush and the American People|location=New York|publisher=Pearson Longman}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Abramowitz|first=Alan I.|year=2010|title=The Disappearing Center: Engaged Citizens, Polarization, and American Democracy|location=New Haven, CT|publisher=Yale University Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Levendusky|first=Matthew|year=2009|title=The Partisan Sort: How Liberals Became Democrats and Conservatives Became Republicans|location=Chicago|publisher=University of Chicago Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Baldassarri|first1=Delia|first2=Andrew|last2=Gelman|year=2008|title=Partisans without Constraint: Political Polarization and Trends in American Public Opinion|journal=American Journal of Sociology|volume=114|issue=2|pages=408–46|jstor=10.1086/590649|doi=10.1086/590649|s2cid=222436264 }}</ref><ref>Fiorina, Morris P., with Samuel J. Abrams and Jeremy C. Pope. (2005). ''Culture War? The Myth of Polarized America.'' New York: Pearson Longman. {{ISBN|978-0205779888}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Hetherington|first=Marc J.|s2cid=14760921|year=2001|title=Resurgent Mass Partisanship: The Role of Elite Polarization|journal=American Political Science Review|volume=95|issue=3|pages=619–631|jstor=3118237|doi=10.1017/s0003055401003045}}</ref> Contemporary political polarization has had important political consequences on American public policy, as Poole and Rosenthal (with fellow political scientist [[Nolan McCarty]]) show in their 2006 book ''Polarized America: The Dance of Ideology and Unequal Riches''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=McCarty |first1=Nolan |url= |title=Polarized America: The Dance of Ideology and Unequal Riches |last2=Poole |first2=Keith T. |last3=Rosenthal |first3=Howard |publisher=MIT Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-262-13464-4 |location=Cambridge, MA}}</ref>

==Applications==
NOMINATE has been used to test, refine, and/or develop wide-ranging theories and models of the United States Congress.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Kiewiet|first1=D. Roderick|first2=Matthew D.|last2=McCubbins|year=1991|title=The Logic of Delegation|location=Chicago|publisher=University of Chicago Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Shickler|first=Eric|year=2000|title=Institutional Change in the House of Representatives, 1867–1998: A Test of Partisan and Ideological Power Balance Models|journal=American Political Science Review|volume=94|issue=2|pages=269–288|jstor=2586012|doi=10.2307/2586012|s2cid=144490248 }}</ref> In ''Ideology and Congress'' (pp.&nbsp;270–271), Poole and Rosenthal agree that their findings are consistent with the "party cartel" model that Cox and McCubbins present in their 1993 book ''Legislative Leviathan''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Cox|first1=Gary W.|first2=Matthew D.|last2=McCubbins|year=1993|title=Legislative Leviathan|location=Berkeley|publisher=University of California Press}}</ref> Keith Krehbiel utilizes NOMINATE scores to determine the ideological rank order of both chambers of Congress in developing his "pivotal politics" theory,<ref>{{cite book|last=Krehbiel|first=Keith|year=1998|title=Pivotal Politics: A Theory of U.S. Lawmaking|url=https://archive.org/details/pivotalpoliticst00kreh|url-access=registration|location=Chicago|publisher=University of Chicago Press}}</ref> as do Gary Cox and Matthew McCubbins in their tests of whether parties in Congress meet the conditions of responsible party government (RPG).<ref>{{cite book|last1=Cox|first1=Gary W.|first2=Matthew D.|last2=McCubbins|year=2005|title=Setting the Agenda: Responsible Party Government in the U.S. House of Representatives|location=New York|publisher=Cambridge University Press}}</ref>

NOMINATE scores have been used by popular media outlets like ''The New York Times'' and ''The Washington Post'' as a measure of the political ideology of political institutions and elected officials or candidates. Political blogger [[Nate Silver]] and his team at [[FiveThirtyEight]] have repeatedly used DW-NOMINATE scores to gauge the ideological location of major political figures and institutions.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/are-sanders-and-cruz-really-less-electable/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160404222435/http://fivethirtyeight.com/features/are-sanders-and-cruz-really-less-electable/|archive-date=4 April 2016|title=Are Sanders And Cruz Really Less 'Electable'?|last=Azari|first=Julia|author-link=Julia Azari|date=4 April 2016|work=[[FiveThirtyEight]]|access-date=24 December 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://fivethirtyeight.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/04/10/an-imbalanced-budget-deal/|title=An Imbalanced Budget Deal?|last=Silver|first=Nate|date=10 April 2011|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=9 November 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://fivethirtyeight.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/09/01/in-targeting-murkowski-tea-party-chooses-wisely/|title=In Singling Out Murkowski, Tea Party Chose Wisely|last=Silver|first=Nate|date=1 September 2010|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=9 November 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://fivethirtyeight.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/04/29/how-liberal-is-president-obama/|title=How Liberal Is President Obama?|last=Silver|first=Nate|date=29 April 2011|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=9 November 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://voices.washingtonpost.com/ezra-klein/2010/08/the_republicans_on_the_deficit.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121014200054/http://voices.washingtonpost.com/ezra-klein/2010/08/the_republicans_on_the_deficit.html|archive-date=14 October 2012|title=The Republicans on the deficit commission are more conservative than the Democrats are liberal|last=Klein|first=Ezra|date=30 August 2008|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=9 November 2012}}</ref>

NOMINATE procedures and related roll call scaling techniques have also been applied to a number of other legislative bodies besides the [[United States Congress]]. These include the [[United Nations General Assembly]],<ref>{{cite journal|author-link1=Erik Voeten|last=Voeten|first=Erik|year=2001|title=Outside Options and the Logic of Security Council Action|journal=American Political Science Review|volume=95|issue=4|pages=845–858|jstor=3117717|doi=10.1017/s000305540101005x}}</ref> [[European Parliament|the European Parliament]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hix|first1=Simon|first2=Abdul|last2=Noury|first3=Gérard|last3=Roland|year=2006|title=Dimensions of Politics in the European Parliament|journal=American Journal of Political Science|volume=50|issue=2|pages=494–511|jstor=3694286|doi=10.1111/j.1540-5907.2006.00198.x|s2cid=56074538 |url=https://escholarship.org/content/qt4gb278j5/qt4gb278j5.pdf?t=krndmb}}</ref> National Assemblies in [[Latin America]],<ref>Mogernstern, Scott. (2004). ''Patterns of Legislative Politics: Roll-Call Voting in Latin America and the United States.'' New York: Cambridge University Press.</ref> and the [[French Fourth Republic]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rosenthal|first1=Howard|first2=Erik|last2=Voeten|year=2004|title=Analyzing Roll Calls with Perfect Spatial Voting: France 1946–1958|journal=American Journal of Political Science|volume=48|issue=3|pages=620–632|doi=10.2307/1519920|jstor=1519920}}</ref> Poole and Rosenthal note in Chapter 11 of ''Ideology and Congress'' (2007) that most of these analyses find that roll call voting is organized by only few dimensions (usually two): "These findings suggest that the need to form parliamentary majorities limits dimensionality."<ref>Poole and Rosenthal, ''Ideology and Congress'', p. 295.</ref>
